why.C: 4/7 leaves one fourteenth too much; the crew painted 7/14.

why.D: 46 is 32 + 14, growing the increase by 4 instead of 3.

items.prompt: After donating 3/8 of a collection, Sam has 45 cards left. How many cards were in the collection at first?

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: Which statement best explains what the students learned from the moth survey?

items.explanation: The problem, the revision and the lesson are all in [¶2–¶4]. Saying pond insects are always harder to photograph makes a rule out of one detail; moving to daylight contradicts the night survey, which worked once the lamps matched; and the brightest lamp is the very condition that made the first comparison unfair.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: [¶3] says several pond species were hard to see until they settled, which is one evening's observation rather than a rule about every pond insect.
why.B: The night survey worked once the lamps matched; daylight is never suggested.
why.C: The brighter lamp is what made the first comparison unfair — the problem, not the method.

items.prompt: Why were the students unable to compare the first station counts fairly?

items.prompt: What can be inferred about the identical lights used in the second count?

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Identical lamps make the stations comparable; they cannot guarantee that nothing was missed.

why.D: Photographing each visitor is the method throughout, and nothing replaces it.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: Which choice best connects the roof's function with the students' investigation?

choices.A: Students discover that every school bus shelter should be built of wood.
choices.B: A leaking shelter roof creates a safety problem for waiting students.
choices.C: A planted roof manages rainwater and teaches students about starting conditions.
choices.D: The environmental club replaces the school's bus shelter after three storms.

items.explanation: The planted-roof summary combines the roof's function [¶2] with the students' learning [¶3–¶4]. Building every shelter of wood and replacing the shelter are unsupported—the club measured rather than rebuilt—and the leaking roof mistakes delayed release for a leak.
items.misconceptions: accepts first assumption; focuses on one material
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Wood never comes up; the roof is covered with shallow trays of low-growing plants.
why.B: [¶2] says it was working as designed, so the dripping was not a leak.
why.D: The club measures and then plans a comparison; it rebuilds nothing.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: Why did the largest storm not fill the barrel the most?

choices.A: Dry soil absorbed much of its rain.
choices.B: Students emptied the barrel during the storm.
choices.C: The plants blocked every drainage channel.
choices.D: Strong wind blew the barrel onto its side.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Nobody empties the barrel; the students measure what is in it after each storm.
why.C: The channels released water slowly, which is how the roof is meant to work.
why.D: Windy days are mentioned as what dried the soil, not as something that moved the barrel.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: Why will the club compare two shelters in spring?

choices.A: To determine which shelter has more students waiting beneath it
choices.B: To find out whether a bare metal roof can collect any rain
choices.C: To prove that the planted shelter never becomes warm in spring
choices.D: To isolate whether the planted roof is related to temperature

items.explanation: Comparing planted and unplanted shelters provides a reference for the temperature question in [¶4]. Counting students and testing whether bare metal collects any rain ask different questions, and proving the planted shelter never becomes warm claims proof before evidence.
items.misconceptions: confuses prediction with proof; misses comparison purpose
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: How many students wait under each shelter has nothing to do with temperature.
why.B: [¶2] already says a bare metal roof sends most water rushing off at once.
why.C: The club predicts the planted roof may be cooler, and a prediction is not a proof.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: In line 20, “runoff” most nearly means:

choices.A: soil carried away by strong wind
choices.B: water that flows off a surface
choices.D: a test that ends too early

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Wind appears only as what dried the soil; this word is about water leaving a surface.
why.C: The plants stay in their shallow trays throughout.

items.prompt: Why does the author include the students' future temperature study in the fourth paragraph (lines 21–27)?

choices.A: To show that recording conditions can guide a new investigation
choices.B: To prove that the school's rain barrel was installed incorrectly

choices.D: To explain why spring storms are heavier than winter storms

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: A reading drive collected 4,608 books in spring and 2,795 in fall. How many books were collected altogether?
items.explanation: 4,608 + 2,795 = 7,403; 7,393 and 7,503 reflect carrying errors, and 6,403 drops one thousand.
items.misconceptions: regrouping error; place-value omission
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: 7,393 is 10 short: the units make 8 + 5 = 13, so a ten carries into 0 + 9 and that column reaches 10.
why.C: 6,403 is 1,000 short; the hundreds make 6 + 7 + 1 = 14, which carries a thousand into 4 + 2.
why.D: 7,503 is 100 over; the hundreds column comes to 14, leaving a 4.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: What is 7/8 − 1/3?
items.explanation: With denominator 24, 21/24 − 8/24 = 13/24.
items.misconceptions: subtracts denominators; fails to find common denominator
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: 6/5 subtracts the denominators as well as the numerators, (7 − 1)/(8 − 3); once the denominators match, only the numerators are subtracted.
why.B: 5/8 keeps eighths and takes something other than 1/3 away from them; over 24, 1/3 is 8/24, not 2/24.
why.D: 4/5 uses a denominator that 8 and 3 do not share; the smallest they do share is 24.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: Six identical notebooks cost $4.75 each. What is the total cost?
items.misconceptions: decimal placement; repeated-addition error
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: 24.75 multiplies only the dollars, 4 × 6 = 24, and then puts the 75 cents back once instead of six times.
why.C: 28.05 has the dollars right and the cents digits swapped; 0.75 × 6 = 4.50, so the cents end in .50.
why.D: 30.75 rounds $4.75 up to $5 for $30 and then adds the 75 cents back — but rounding up had already added 25 cents six times.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: A printer places 945 cards equally into 15 boxes. How many cards are in each box?
items.explanation: 945 ÷ 15 = 63 because 15 × 63 = 945; the other choices come from incomplete division or rounding.
items.misconceptions: division regrouping; estimate used as exact answer
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: 53 is ten too few: 15 × 53 = 795, a full 150 short of 945.
why.B: 60 gives 15 × 60 = 900, leaving 45 still to share — three more per box.
why.C: 65 overshoots: 15 × 65 = 975.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: A 160-page book has illustrations on 45% of its pages. How many pages have illustrations?
items.explanation: 45% of 160: 10% is 16, so 40% is 64 and 5% is 8, together 72.
items.misconceptions: uses a nearby benchmark percent; finds the complement
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: 56 is 35% of 160, a nearby percent.
why.B: 64 is 40% of 160, rounding 45% down.
why.D: 88 is 55% of 160, the pages without illustrations.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: What is the greatest common factor of 36 and 54?
items.explanation: Common factors include 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, and 18; 18 is greatest. 9 and 6 are common but not greatest, and 108 is a multiple.
items.misconceptions: stops at smaller factor; confuses factor and multiple
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: 9 is a common factor but not the greatest; 18 divides both numbers as well.
why.C: 6 is common and smaller still; 18 goes into 36 and 54 too.
why.D: 108 is a common multiple of 36 and 54, not a factor of either.

items.subject: MA
items.explanation: 1/4 + 2/3 = 3/12 + 8/12 = 11/12, and whole parts total 5. The distractors add denominators or regroup incorrectly.
items.misconceptions: adds denominators; unnecessary regrouping
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: 5 3/7 adds the tops and the bottoms of the fractions; quarters and thirds both go over 12 first.
why.B: 6 1/12 carries a whole that is not there: 3/12 + 8/12 = 11/12, still under 1.
why.C: 5 5/12 changes 1/4 to 3/12 but then adds 2/3 as if it were 2/12; 2/3 is 8/12.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: Which fraction is equal to 0.625?
items.explanation: 0.625 = 625/1000 = 5/8; 3/5 and 5/6 are nearby values, and 625/10 places the decimal incorrectly.
items.misconceptions: denominator place-value error; chooses nearby familiar fraction
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: 3/5 is 0.6 — close, but 0.625 is 625/1000, which reduces to 5/8.
why.C: 5/6 is about 0.833, well above 0.625.
why.D: 625/10 is 62.5; three decimal places make 0.625 into 625/1000.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: Solve 5x + 7 = 42.
items.explanation: Subtract 7 from both sides to get 5x = 35, then divide by 5 for x = 7.
items.misconceptions: wrong inverse-operation order; treats constant as factor
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: 5 divides 35 by the 7 rather than by the 5; the 5 is what multiplies x.
why.C: 9 follows from taking 42 − 7 as 45; it is 35, and 35 ÷ 5 = 7.
why.D: 49/5 adds the 7 to 42 instead of subtracting it; a + 7 moves across as − 7.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: What is the value of 3x² − 5 when x = 4?
items.explanation: 4² = 16, then 3 × 16 − 5 = 43. 19 squares after multiplying incorrectly, and 31 and 37 reflect arithmetic errors.
items.misconceptions: ignores exponent; performs subtraction too early
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: 19 comes from taking 4² as 8 — doubling instead of squaring. 4² is 16, so 3 × 16 − 5 = 43.
why.B: 31 is not 3 × 16 − 5; squaring the 4 first gives 16, and 48 − 5 = 43.
why.C: 37 falls six short: 3 × 16 = 48, then take away 5.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: Which expression is equivalent to 4(n + 5)?
items.explanation: Multiply both terms inside by 4: 4 × n and 4 × 5, which is 4n + 20.
items.misconceptions: partial distribution; combines a number and a variable
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: 4n + 5 multiplies only the n by 4; the 5 inside the parentheses is multiplied too.
why.C: 9n adds the 4 and the 5, but the 4 multiplies the whole bracket.
why.D: 20n multiplies 4 × 5 and attaches the n, as if the bracket were 5n.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: Which inequality is equivalent to n/4 < 6?
items.explanation: Multiplying both sides by positive 4 gives n < 24; n > 24 reverses the sign, and n < 2 and n > 10 use wrong operations.
items.misconceptions: reverses inequality unnecessarily; divides instead of multiplies
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: n < 2 divides where it should multiply; n/4 < 6 means n is under 4 × 6.
why.B: n > 24 reverses the sign; multiplying both sides by a positive 4 leaves the direction alone.
why.D: n > 10 reverses the sign and uses 4 + 6 rather than 4 × 6.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: Two angles of a triangle measure 48° and 67°. What is the third angle?
items.explanation: Triangle angles total 180°; 180 − (48 + 67) = 65°. The distractors reflect addition or subtraction errors.
items.misconceptions: uses wrong angle sum; arithmetic error
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: 55 subtracts 125 from 180; 48 + 67 is 115.
why.B: 61 falls four short: 180 − 115 = 65.
why.C: 63 is two short; the two known angles total 115, not 117.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: A parallelogram has a base of 13 cm and a perpendicular height of 8 cm. What is its area?
items.explanation: Area = base × perpendicular height = 13 × 8 = 104 cm².
items.misconceptions: uses slanted side; confuses area and perimeter
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: 42 is 2 × (13 + 8), a perimeter; area multiplies the base by the height.
why.C: 84 is not 13 × 8; multiplying those out gives 104.
why.D: 208 is 13 × 8 × 2, the area counted twice; a parallelogram needs no doubling or halving.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: A circular table has a diameter of 18 feet. What is its radius?
items.explanation: Radius is half the diameter, so 18 ÷ 2 = 9 feet.
items.misconceptions: swaps radius and diameter; applies wrong factor
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: 36 is 18 × 2, doubling the diameter instead of halving it.
why.B: 18 is the diameter itself; a radius reaches only from the centre to the edge.
why.D: 6 is 18 ÷ 3; a radius is half the diameter, not a third.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: A storage box is 7 feet long, 4 feet wide, and 3 feet high. What is its volume?
items.explanation: Volume = 7 × 4 × 3 = 84 cubic feet. 28 ft³ multiplies only length and width (7 × 4), while 42 ft³ and 98 ft³ first add all three dimensions (7 + 4 + 3 = 14) and then multiply by the height (14 × 3 = 42) or the length (14 × 7 = 98) instead of multiplying all three dimensions.
items.misconceptions: computes base area only; omits a dimension
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: 28 is 7 × 4, the floor of the box; volume multiplies that by the height of 3.
why.C: 42 is 14 × 3, adding the three dimensions (7 + 4 + 3) and then multiplying by the height.
why.D: 98 is 14 × 7, adding the three dimensions and then multiplying by the length.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: A ribbon is 3.6 meters long. How many centimeters long is it?
items.explanation: One meter is 100 centimeters, so 3.6 × 100 = 360 cm.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: 3.6 cm keeps the number and only changes the unit; a meter is 100 centimeters.
why.B: 36 cm multiplies by 10 instead of 100.
why.D: 36,000 cm multiplies by 10,000, two place shifts too many.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: A workshop begins at 3:40 p.m. and lasts 2 hours 35 minutes. When does it end?
items.explanation: 3:40 + 2 hours = 5:40, plus 35 minutes = 6:15. The distractors omit time or fail to regroup 60 minutes.

why.A: 5:15 adds 1 hour 35 rather than 2 hours 35.
why.B: 5:55 adds only 15 minutes past 5:40; there are 35 to add.
why.C: 6:05 adds 25 minutes past 5:40 rather than 35.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: What is the mean of 12, 15, 17, 20, and 26?
items.explanation: The sum is 90, and 90 ÷ 5 = 18.
items.misconceptions: confuses mean and median; arithmetic error
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: 16 would need a total of 80; the five numbers add to 90.
why.B: 17 is the middle number, the median, not the mean.
why.D: 19 would need a total of 95; the numbers add to 90.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: A fair spinner is numbered 1 through 8. What is the probability of spinning an even number?
items.explanation: Four of eight outcomes—2, 4, 6, 8—are even, so 4/8 = 1/2. The distractors miscount favorable outcomes.
items.misconceptions: counts prime numbers; forgets to simplify
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: 1/4 counts two even numbers; from 1 to 8 there are four — 2, 4, 6 and 8.
why.C: 3/8 counts three; 8 itself is even, which makes four.
why.D: 5/8 counts five, one more than there are.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: The number of minutes spent practicing over seven days was 18, 24, 18, 30, 21, 18, and 27. What is the mode?
items.explanation: Eighteen appears three times, more than any other value. 21, 24 and 30 each appear once — the mode is the value that turns up most often, not the largest or the last.
items.misconceptions: confuses mode with median or maximum; ignores frequency
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: 21 appears once, and the mode is the value that appears most often.
why.B: 24 also appears just once.
why.C: 30 is the largest value and appears once; the mode is about frequency, not size.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: In which quadrant is the point (−5, −2)?
items.explanation: A negative x-coordinate and negative y-coordinate place the point in Quadrant III. The others correspond to different sign pairs.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Quadrant I has both coordinates positive.
why.B: Quadrant II has a negative x and a positive y, and here y is −2.
why.D: Quadrant IV has a positive x and a negative y, and here x is −5.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a regular pentagon have?
items.explanation: Each vertex-to-opposite-side-midpoint axis gives one line, for 5 total.
items.misconceptions: confuses sides with pairs; assumes odd-sided shapes lack symmetry
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: 1 counts a single axis; a regular pentagon has one through each of its five vertices.
why.C: 10 counts every axis twice, once from the vertex and once from the midpoint, but it is the same line both ways.
why.D: 0 would be right for an irregular pentagon; a regular one has five equal sides and five axes.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: A 10-by-8-meter rectangular patio has a 3-by-2-meter rectangular garden removed from one corner. What is the remaining patio area?
items.explanation: Full area is 80 m² and removed area is 6 m², leaving 74 m². 80 m² ignores the removal, and 68 m² and 70 m² subtract dimensions or the wrong area.

items.subject: MA
items.prompt: Which is the prime factorization of 180?
items.explanation: 180 = 4 × 45 = 2² × 3² × 5, and all factors are prime. 2 × 3 × 30, 2² × 45 and 3² × 20 each still leave a composite factor — 30, 45 and 20 — so none of them is a full prime factorization.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: 2 × 3 × 30 does make 180, but 30 is not prime — it is 2 × 3 × 5.
why.C: 2² × 45 leaves 45, which is 3 × 3 × 5.
why.D: 3² × 20 leaves 20, which is 2 × 2 × 5.

items.prompt: A class uses 3/5 of 45 sheets of paper. Of the sheets used, 2/3 are blue. How many blue sheets are used?

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: 12 is neither step; 3/5 of 45 is 27, and 2/3 of 27 is 18.
why.B: 15 is not 2/3 of 27, which comes to 18.
why.D: 27 comes from taking 3/5 of 45 and stopping there; two thirds of those 27 are blue.

items.prompt: On a drawing, 1 centimeter represents 250 centimeters. A hallway measures 6 centimeters on the drawing. How long is the actual hallway in meters?

items.prompt: Twelve of 30 survey responses chose option A. What percent chose option A?
items.misconceptions: denominator-as-percent; reverses selected and unselected

why.A: 30% is the number of responses, not a percentage of them; 12 out of 30 is 40%.
why.C: 60% is the 18 who chose something else; the question asks about the 12.
